blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given an array prices where prices[i] is the price of a stock on day i, choose a single day to buy and a later single day to sell to maximize profit. Return the maximum profit possible, or 0 if no profit can be made.

blocks.text: Given an array prices where prices[i] is the price of a stock on day i, choose a single day to buy and a later single day to sell to maximize profit. Return the maximum profit possible, or 0 if no profit can be made.

blocks.title: Analogy: Buying Low and Selling High, Once
blocks.text: Like watching a stock ticker for a single trading opportunity: buy on the cheapest day seen so far and sell on the day that gives the best gain over that cheapest price, remembering that a sale can only happen after the purchase, never before it.

blocks.caption: Buy on one day, sell on a later day, maximize the difference

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result"],"rows":[["Buy at price 1 (day index 1)","lowest price seen"],["Sell at price 6 (day index 4)","best later price"],["Answer","6 minus 1 equals 5"]]}

blocks.text: With only a single day of prices, there is no later day available to sell on, so the maximum profit is 0.
It is worth asking, for any single fixed day chosen to sell on, exactly how much information about every earlier day actually needs to be kept.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: For a fixed sell day, the best possible profit only ever depends on the single lowest price among every earlier day, not on each of those earlier prices individually.

Observation 2: That means the whole nested comparison can collapse into a single running summary statistic, the minimum price seen so far, carried forward through one pass, rather than a hash set or a running total.

Observation 3: Testing prices equal to [7, 1, 5, 3, 6, 4] confirms it, the best profit at day index 4, price 6, only ever needs to know that the minimum price among days 0 through 3 was 1, not each of those four individual prices.

Observation 4: On every day, computing today's possible profit against that one running minimum, and keeping the best profit seen, is enough to guarantee the true maximum is found by the end of the pass.
Recognizing that only a single running minimum needs to be carried forward, not the whole history of earlier prices, is what turns a pairwise comparison into a single linear pass.
Check every possible pair of a buy day and a later sell day, computing the profit for each and keeping track of the best one seen.

items: For every day i, consider every later day j.
Compute the profit as prices[j] minus prices[i].
Keep the largest profit seen across every pair, or 0 if every pair is negative.

codes.python:
def max_profit(prices):
    best = 0
    n = len(prices)
    for i in range(n):                                      # every possible buy day
        for j in range(i + 1, n):                             # every possible later sell day
            profit = prices[j] - prices[i]
            best = max(best, profit)                              # keep the best profit seen so far
    return best


if __name__ == "__main__":
    prices = [7, 1, 5, 3, 6, 4]
    print(max_profit(prices))

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: best starts at 0, matching the requirement that a profit of 0 is returned when no pair is genuinely profitable.
The inner loop only considers days strictly after i, so a sell day is never allowed to come before or on the same day as the buy day.
Every pair's profit is compared directly against the running best, with no early exit, since any later pair could still turn out to be the true maximum.

blocks.text: Every valid buy and sell pair is considered, so the best possible profit is guaranteed to be found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), for the nested loop over every pair of days.
Space: O(1), no extra data structure is used.
Limitation: most of these pairs are irrelevant. For a fixed sell day, only the single lowest price seen on any earlier day actually matters, not every earlier price individually.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why checking every pair works but is wasteful: for a given sell day, every earlier day gets compared individually, even though only the single cheapest one among them could ever produce the best profit.

What actually needs to be remembered from everything seen so far: just one number, the lowest price encountered on any earlier day.

Can that one running number replace the entire inner loop: yes, comparing today's price against the running minimum gives exactly the same best-case profit that scanning every earlier day individually would have found.

Does this still correctly forbid selling before buying: yes, the running minimum is only ever updated using days already passed, so any profit computed against it always corresponds to a valid, later sell day.

The core idea: walk the prices once, updating a running minimum price and comparing today's price against it to update the best profit seen.

Walk through the prices once, keeping track of the lowest price seen so far. On every day, compute the profit from selling today against that running minimum, and keep the best profit seen. This removes the need to re-examine every earlier day for each later day.
Track the minimum price seen so far and the best profit found so far in a single pass.

blocks.caption: Optimized: one pass, tracking the running minimum price and the best profit so far

blocks.text: This works because the running minimum, at the moment any given day is reached, always equals the true lowest price among every strictly earlier day, exactly the one value that matters for computing the best possible profit if that day were chosen as the sell day; comparing today's price against that running minimum and updating the best-so-far therefore considers every valid buy-sell pair's best case, without ever comparing against an invalid, later buy day.

blocks.text: This is the simplest member of the "buy low, sell high" family of stock problems, and the running minimum pattern used here (track the best value seen so far, compare everything against it in one pass) reappears throughout array problems that ask for a best pair or best difference.

items: Using the brute force nested loop approach, which is correct but unnecessarily slow for large inputs.
Allowing a sell day to come before or on the same day as the buy day, which the single pass approach naturally avoids since only prices seen so far are ever used as the minimum.

blocks.text: Mention explicitly that this variant only allows a single buy and a single sell, since a very similar looking problem allows unlimited transactions and needs a different approach entirely.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you avoid checking every pair", think: track the running minimum price seen so far, compare every day against just that one value.
If the interviewer says "what if multiple transactions were allowed", think: that is a different problem, requiring a different, more general approach.
If the interviewer says "how do you guarantee the sell day comes after the buy day", think: the running minimum only ever reflects days already passed, so any profit computed against it is automatically valid.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Brute force: O(n squared) time, O(1) space. Optimized: O(n) time, O(1) space.

items: Pattern: single pass tracking a running extremum, the lowest price seen so far, and comparing every new value against that one summary statistic instead of against every earlier value individually.

Core Idea: for a fixed sell day, only the single lowest price among all earlier days matters, so tracking a running minimum and comparing today's price against it, in one pass, finds the same answer a full pairwise comparison would.
Time: O(n squared) for the brute force, O(n) for the optimized version.
Space: O(1) for both versions.
Most Important Observation: a pairwise comparison problem can often collapse into a single running extremum when only the best earlier value, not every earlier value, actually matters.
Interview Difficulty: easy to write the brute force; recognizing that a single running minimum replaces the entire inner loop is what shows real understanding.
One line memory trick: track the running minimum price, compare today against it, keep the best profit seen.
